title: The March 1942 Fire That Nearly Ended Ole Kirk's Toy Business
dek: When his Billund toy factory burned down in wartime Denmark, Ole Kirk Christiansen almost stopped, then borrowed to rebuild on the same site.

story.event: Deciding to rebuild in Billund after fire destroyed the wooden-toy factory
story.summary: On the night of 20 March 1942 a fire destroyed Ole Kirk Christiansen's wooden-toy factory in Billund, Denmark; insurance did not cover the loss and a new building. He almost gave up and received offers to build elsewhere, but stayed in Billund, keeping the jobs of his 26 employees, and rebuilt on the same site with a loan from Vejle Bank. The new, more modern toy factory was finished in 1943 by the company's account.
paragraphs: At three o'clock one morning in March 1942, one of the young men who slept in the workshop in Billund, Denmark, came and shouted to Ole Kirk Christiansen that the factory was burning. In memoirs his company later quoted, he called it "a shocking message – and painful." Struggling to take it in, he wrote, he paused to kneel before God, and that gave him peace of mind. The family home next door was saved. The woodworking factory was not.

He was fifty. In 1932 he had gone bankrupt and lost his wife in the same year, left with four young sons, and he had built a living since on wooden toys made with unusual care: beech air-dried for two years, then kiln-dried for three weeks. The war had helped. With imports halted and metal and rubber barred from toys, the company says, sales doubled in its first two years. Now the building and its stock were gone, and every model and pattern would have to be drawn again by hand. The insurance would not cover both the loss and a new factory.

According to the company's history, he almost gave up. Offers came from other parts of Denmark to build a factory there instead. He chose to stay in Billund, keeping the jobs of his 26 employees, and the company says it was his sense of responsibility for his sons and staff that persuaded him. Vejle Bank agreed to lend him the money. With family and employees helping, a new factory went up on the site of the old workshop, built from the start for making toys.

Production restarted before the end of the year, by the company's account, in a building more modern than the old one and better suited to making toys in quantity. LEGO dates its completion to 1943; other accounts say it opened in 1944. After the war the company bought a plastic injection-moulding machine, and by the time Ole Kirk died in 1958, plastic building bricks had become its great success.

quote.text: It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius likens steady learning to raising a mound on bare, level ground: one basketful at a time, each still counting as going forward. Ole Kirk began again on a burnt site, redrawing every model and pattern by hand before the new factory could make anything.

reflection: By his own account, when Ole Kirk heard the factory was burning, his first response was not to act but to stop, kneel and find some quiet. The decisions came afterwards: whether to carry on, where, and for whom. What settled them, the company says, was the 26 people whose work depended on his.

When something you have built is damaged, whether a lost file, a failed plan or simply a hard week, the pull is to fix it at once. A pause first is not time lost. It can be what lets you see who is affected, what is worth rebuilding as it was, and what is better rebuilt differently.
invitation: If something of yours has recently gone wrong, take five quiet minutes before touching it today. Then write down one person it affects and one thing you would build differently this time.

cross_checks.claim: In 1942 fire destroyed the factory in Billund and it was rebuilt there
He nearly gave up and rebuilt out of a sense of responsibility to his workers
The timber was air-dried for two years and kiln-dried for three weeks
In 1932 he went bankrupt and his wife died, leaving him with four young sons
The new factory was completed in 1943 (company) or opened in 1944 (other accounts)

research_notes: Headcount differs: LEGO's history says the decision to stay saved the jobs of 26 employees and, on a second page, that the company employed 40 people the year after the fire; Dansk Biografisk Leksikon gives about 25 employees at the end of the war; Wikipedia's timeline (not cited) gives 29 in 1943. The story uses only the company's 26 at the time of the fire and does not give a later headcount. Completion of the new factory: LEGO says 1943 (with production resumed by the end of 1942); History Hit and Wikipedia say it opened in 1944 with an assembly line; the story gives both. Date: LEGO says 'during the night of March 20, 1942' and the memoir puts the alarm at three in the morning, so the story says 'three o'clock one morning in March 1942' and the summary 'the night of 20 March'; a fan wiki gives 22 March (not used). Cause: History Hit and Wikipedia say a short circuit; LEGO gives no cause; the story does not state one. Plastic moulding machine: HISTORY says 1946 and History Hit 1947, so the story says only 'after the war'. The almost-giving-up, the offers from elsewhere, the insurance shortfall and the Vejle Bank loan rest on the company's own history (two LEGO.com pages, one site), with independent support only for the general point that he nearly gave up and rebuilt out of responsibility to his workforce (History Hit). The memoir lines are as quoted in English by LEGO; the memoir itself is not public. LEGO spells his name Kristiansen; Dansk Biografisk Leksikon and most English sources use Christiansen, which the story follows. 'Bootstrapped' here means a family firm financed from its own earnings, family guarantees and a bank loan, with no outside investors. The Analects passage is Confucius on learning; it is applied by analogy.
